title: Labor’s tax twists sink renters into red
full_text:
Low-income renters are bearing the brunt of the nation’s cost-of-living crisis, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has warned, with Labor’s investor tax reforms to hit battlers with “steeper rents, less choice and more competition”.
Speaking at the ASIC Annual Forum in Sydney yesterday, Ms Bullock said that despite 18-year high interest rates of 4.85 per cent, “we should not be worrying” about the “average Australian household budget”, but rather people who are struggling towards the bottom end, noting they are “typically renters” and “typically on low incomes”.
“They are the ones that are having to deal with the cost of living within a budget – and it’s a budget of essentials,” she said.
Independent property economist Cameron Kusher said that Labor’s May budget tax changes to abolish negative gearing on existing properties and change the capital gains tax concession to a model indexed to inflation would reduce the number of property investors and in turn put pressure on rental stock and prices.
While Labor argues its reforms will turn more renters into homeowners, Mr Kusher said “lower-income people are always going to struggle to enter into the housing market”.
“For them, it’s still going to be a challenge. They’re facing steeper rents, less choice and more competition,” he said. “And they don’t have the ability to really exit the rental market.” According to realestate.com.au’s September Rental Report, rents across Australia have increased by 5.5 per cent, year-on-year. Median rents were the highest in Sydney at $800.
Minutes from the Reserve Bank’s November meeting, where it hiked rates for the fifth time this year, noted concern from board members that the “decline in housing turnover would reduce economic activity”. The RBA also noted that “the decline in lending for new housing had been pronounced for investors, in part reflecting recent tax changes”.
A spokesman for Housing Minister Clare O’Neil acknowledged that “renters are doing it really tough” but said Commonwealth Rent Assistance had been boosted by more than 50 per cent. He also said the removal of “generous tax concessions” would ensure “the 400 per cent increase in house prices we saw over the last 25 years isn’t replicated”.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said Labor’s tax reforms had “tanked the housing market”.
“Only this Prime Minister and his hapless Treasurer could hand down a budget designed to improve housing affordability which does the exact opposite,” he said. “Rents are up, investment is down, confidence is smashed, and it’s harder than ever for young Australians to buy their first home.” Parramatta locals Sean Koh and Veronica Chin said they were struggling to stay afloat as soaring rents, electricity prices and grocery bills squeezed their finances, despite working four jobs between them. “The financial stress really starts to hit you,” Mr Koh said.
